claim: Cortical access tissue samples from eight individuals who underwent clinically indicated neurosurgical procedures were experimentally assessed in this study.
source: Cortical access tissue samples from eight individuals who underwent clinically indicated neurosurgical procedures, such as for tumors or epilepsy, were experimentally assessed in this study (details provided in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and source of human tissue samples used.

claim: Acute cortical slices were treated for 6–10 hr with atRA (1 µM) or vehicle-only.
source: Acute cortical slices were treated for 6–10 hr with atRA (1 µM) or vehicle-only, and superficial (layer 2/3) pyramidal neurons were recorded in a whole-cell configuration (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental treatment protocol.

claim: No significant differences in active or passive membrane properties were detected between atRA-treated and vehicle-only groups in human cortical neurons.
source: While no significant differences in active or passive membrane properties were detected between the two groups (Figure 1C–E), a robust increase in the amplitudes of glutamate (i.e., α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid, AMPA) receptor-mediated spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) was observed in the atRA-treated slices (Figure 1F,G; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological measurements comparing treatment groups.

claim: A robust increase in the amplitudes of AMPA receptor-mediated spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) was observed in the atRA-treated slices.
source: While no significant differences in active or passive membrane properties were detected between the two groups (Figure 1C–E), a robust increase in the amplitudes of glutamate (i.e., α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid, AMPA) receptor-mediated spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) was observed in the atRA-treated slices (Figure 1F,G; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript presents electrophysiological data showing increased sEPSC amplitudes.

claim: The mean sEPSC frequency was not significantly different between atRA-treated and vehicle-only groups.
source: The mean sEPSC frequency was not significantly different between the two groups (Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of sEPSC frequency measurements.

claim: atRA mediates a strengthening of excitatory neurotransmission onto human cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: These results demonstrate an atRA-mediated strengthening of excitatory neurotransmission onto human cortical pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the increased sEPSC amplitude data.

claim: A positive correlation between excitatory synaptic strength (sEPSC amplitude) and dendritic spine size has been demonstrated in various animal models.
source: A positive correlation between excitatory synaptic strength, that is, sEPSC amplitude, and dendritic spine size has been demonstrated in various animal models (Bosch and Hayashi, 2012; Matsuzaki et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies establishing this correlation.

claim: No significant differences in spine density were observed between atRA-treated and vehicle-only groups.
source: No significant differences in spine density were observed between the two groups (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports morphological analysis of dendritic spines.

claim: Marked increases in spine head sizes were evident in the atRA-treated group.
source: However, marked increases in spine head sizes were evident in the atRA-treated group (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript presents morphological measurements of spine head size.

claim: Excitatory synaptic strength (sEPSC amplitude) is positively correlated with dendritic spine size in human cortical pyramidal cells.
source: These findings identify that excitatory synaptic strength, as indicated by sEPSC amplitudes, is positively correlated with dendritic spine size in human cortical pyramidal cells, thus revealing coordinated structural and functional changes of excitatory postsynaptic membranes in atRA-treated human cortical slices.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the combined electrophysiological and morphological data.

claim: atRA induces coordinated structural and functional changes of excitatory postsynaptic membranes in human cortical slices.
source: These findings identify that excitatory synaptic strength, as indicated by sEPSC amplitudes, is positively correlated with dendritic spine size in human cortical pyramidal cells, thus revealing coordinated structural and functional changes of excitatory postsynaptic membranes in atRA-treated human cortical slices.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on combined structural and functional data.

claim: Synaptopodin is an actin-modulating protein.
source: In this context, we also evaluated the role of the actin-modulating protein synaptopodin (Mundel et al., 1997), an essential component of the spine apparatus organelle (Deller et al., 2003), which is a key regulator of synaptic plasticity in the rodent brain (Deller et al., 2003; Segal et al., 2010; Vlachos et al., 2013) and has recently been linked to the cognitive trajectory in human aging (Wingo et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work characterizing synaptopodin.

claim: Synaptopodin is an essential component of the spine apparatus organelle.
source: In this context, we also evaluated the role of the actin-modulating protein synaptopodin (Mundel et al., 1997), an essential component of the spine apparatus organelle (Deller et al., 2003), which is a key regulator of synaptic plasticity in the rodent brain (Deller et al., 2003; Segal et al., 2010; Vlachos et al., 2013) and has recently been linked to the cognitive trajectory in human aging (Wingo et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work establishing synaptopodin's role.

claim: The spine apparatus organelle is a key regulator of synaptic plasticity in the rodent brain.
source: In this context, we also evaluated the role of the actin-modulating protein synaptopodin (Mundel et al., 1997), an essential component of the spine apparatus organelle (Deller et al., 2003), which is a key regulator of synaptic plasticity in the rodent brain (Deller et al., 2003; Segal et al., 2010; Vlachos et al., 2013) and has recently been linked to the cognitive trajectory in human aging (Wingo et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on spine apparatus function.

claim: Synaptopodin has been linked to the cognitive trajectory in human aging.
source: In this context, we also evaluated the role of the actin-modulating protein synaptopodin (Mundel et al., 1997), an essential component of the spine apparatus organelle (Deller et al., 2003), which is a key regulator of synaptic plasticity in the rodent brain (Deller et al., 2003; Segal et al., 2010; Vlachos et al., 2013) and has recently been linked to the cognitive trajectory in human aging (Wingo et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a recent study linking synaptopodin to human aging.

claim: 74 ± 2% of all dendritic spines contained a synaptopodin cluster in human superficial (layer 2/3) pyramidal neurons.
source: Synaptopodin clusters were detected in a considerable number of dendritic spines of human superficial (layer 2/3) pyramidal neurons: 74 ± 2% of all dendritic spines contained a synaptopodin cluster in a characteristic position, that is, in the base, neck, or head of the spine (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative immunofluorescence data.

claim: Synaptopodin clusters are located in characteristic positions in dendritic spines (base, neck, or head).
source: Synaptopodin clusters were detected in a considerable number of dendritic spines of human superficial (layer 2/3) pyramidal neurons: 74 ± 2% of all dendritic spines contained a synaptopodin cluster in a characteristic position, that is, in the base, neck, or head of the spine (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the spatial distribution of synaptopodin in spines.

claim: There is a positive correlation between synaptopodin cluster size and spine head size in the human cortex.
source: Similar to previous reports (Holbro et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2009; Yap et al., 2020), we also observed a positive correlation between synaptopodin cluster size and spine head size in the human cortex (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation analysis of morphological measurements.

claim: Synaptopodin-positive spines are significantly larger than their synaptopodin-negative neighbors.
source: Finally, synaptopodin-positive spines were significantly larger than their synaptopodin-negative neighbors (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative morphological analysis.

claim: Synaptopodin clusters are found in strategic positions in a subset of large dendritic spines of the adult human cortex.
source: Hence, this study reveals that synaptopodin clusters are found in strategic positions in a subset of large dendritic spines of the adult human cortex.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings about synaptopodin localization.

claim: atRA does not act specifically on synaptopodin-containing spines.
source: Systematic assessment of synaptopodin-positive and synaptopodin-negative spines revealed that atRA does not act specifically on synaptopodin-containing spines (Figure 2F); in fact, significant atRA-mediated increases in spine head size were observed in both synaptopodin-positive and -negative dendritic spines.
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative analysis of spine subpopulations.

claim: Significant atRA-mediated increases in spine head size were observed in both synaptopodin-positive and -negative dendritic spines.
source: Systematic assessment of synaptopodin-positive and synaptopodin-negative spines revealed that atRA does not act specifically on synaptopodin-containing spines (Figure 2F); in fact, significant atRA-mediated increases in spine head size were observed in both synaptopodin-positive and -negative dendritic spines.
evidence: The manuscript reports morphological measurements in spine subpopulations.

claim: atRA caused a significant increase in the sizes of synaptopodin clusters.
source: Although we did not observe a significant difference in the number of synaptopodin-positive spines between the two groups (control: 71 ± 4% in 14 dendritic segments; atRA: 77 ± 2% in 21 dendritic segments; p=0.25, Mann–Whitney test), atRA caused a significant increase in the sizes of synaptopodin clusters (Figure 2G; c.f., Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative analysis of synaptopodin cluster size.

claim: Remodeling of synaptopodin clusters accompanies atRA-mediated coordinated structural and functional changes in human dendritic spines.
source: We conclude that remodeling of synaptopodin clusters accompanies atRA-mediated coordinated structural and functional changes in human dendritic spines.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on combined structural and functional data.

claim: Remodeling of synaptopodin clusters reflects plasticity-related ultrastructural changes in spine apparatus organelles.
source: In an earlier study, we showed that remodeling of synaptopodin clusters reflects plasticity-related ultrastructural changes in spine apparatus organelles (Vlachos et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work linking synaptopodin to spine apparatus.

claim: Synaptopodin is a marker of the human spine apparatus organelle.
source: After confirming that synaptopodin is a marker of the human spine apparatus organelle using pre-embedding immunogold labeling techniques (Figure 2H), the ultrastructural properties of this organelle were assessed in cross-sectional transmission electron micrographs of 103 control and 114 atRA-treated asymmetric spine synapses from three independent samples (Figure 2I,J).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunogold electron microscopy data.

claim: A marked increase in the cross-sectional area of the spine apparatus organelle was observed in the atRA-treated group.
source: A marked increase in the cross-sectional area of the spine apparatus organelle was observed in the atRA-treated group, which is consistent with the atRA-induced increase in synaptopodin cluster size (Figure 2J; positive correlations between spine apparatus cross-sections and spine cross-sections are shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy measurements.

claim: Changes in the structural and functional properties of dendritic spines are accompanied by ultrastructural changes in spine apparatus organelles.
source: Taken together, these results reveal a link between synaptopodin and the spine apparatus organelle in the human cortex. Specifically, these findings demonstrate that changes in the structural and functional properties of dendritic spines are accompanied by ultrastructural changes in spine apparatus organelles.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on combined structural and ultrastructural data.

claim: atRA is a potent mediator of coordinated (ultra)structural and functional synaptic changes in the adult human cortex.
source: We conclude that atRA is a potent mediator of coordinated (ultra)structural and functional synaptic changes in the adult human cortex.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on the totality of experimental findings.

claim: Synaptopodin-deficient mice lack spine apparatus organelles.
source: Synaptopodin-deficient mice lack spine apparatus organelles and exhibit defects in synaptic plasticity and behavioral learning (Deller et al., 2003; Jedlicka et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work characterizing the knockout mouse model.

claim: Synaptopodin-deficient mice exhibit defects in synaptic plasticity and behavioral learning.
source: Synaptopodin-deficient mice lack spine apparatus organelles and exhibit defects in synaptic plasticity and behavioral learning (Deller et al., 2003; Jedlicka et al., 2009; Vlachos et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on the knockout mouse phenotype.

claim: Changes in excitatory neurotransmission in mouse superficial pyramidal neurons are similar to what was observed in human cortical slices following atRA treatment.
source: Single-cell recordings of superficial (layer 2/3) pyramidal neurons from Synpo+/+ slices showed that changes in excitatory neurotransmission are similar to what we observed in the human cortical slices: sEPSC amplitudes (but not frequencies) were significantly increased following atRA treatment (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The manuscript compares electrophysiological data from mouse and human experiments.

claim: sEPSC amplitudes (but not frequencies) were significantly increased following atRA treatment in wild-type mouse cortical neurons.
source: Single-cell recordings of superficial (layer 2/3) pyramidal neurons from Synpo+/+ slices showed that changes in excitatory neurotransmission are similar to what we observed in the human cortical slices: sEPSC amplitudes (but not frequencies) were significantly increased following atRA treatment (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological measurements in mouse neurons.

claim: atRA reduced the input resistance of wild-type mouse pyramidal cells.
source: Notably, atRA also reduced the input resistance of these pyramidal cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological measurements of passive properties.

claim: The resting membrane potentials and action potential frequencies were not affected by atRA in wild-type mouse neurons.
source: The resting membrane potentials and action potential (AP) frequencies were not affected by atRA, similar to what we observed in the human cortical slices (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; c.f., Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological measurements comparing treatment groups.

claim: atRA exerts comparable effects on excitatory neurotransmission in both the adult mouse and human neocortex.
source: We conclude that atRA exerts comparable effects on excitatory neurotransmission in both the adult mouse and human neocortex.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on comparative data from mouse and human experiments.

claim: No significant changes in sEPSC properties were observed following atRA treatment in synaptopodin-deficient preparations.
source: In Synpo−/− preparations, no significant changes in sEPSC properties were observed following atRA treatment (Figure 3C,D), thus demonstrating the relevance of synaptopodin in atRA-mediated synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological data from knockout mice.

claim: The presence of synaptopodin is required for atRA-mediated synaptic plasticity.
source: In Synpo−/− preparations, no significant changes in sEPSC properties were observed following atRA treatment (Figure 3C,D), thus demonstrating the relevance of synaptopodin in atRA-mediated synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the lack of effect in knockout mice.

claim: A reduction in the input resistance was not observed in atRA-treated synaptopodin-deficient preparations.
source: Additionally, a reduction in the input resistance was not observed in atRA-treated Synpo−/− preparations (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological measurements in knockout mice.

claim: The active and passive membrane properties of wild-type and synaptopodin-deficient neurons were indistinguishable.
source: Furthermore, the active and passive membrane properties of Synpo+/+ and Synpo−/− neurons were indistinguishable (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), despite significant increases in the baseline sEPSC properties of Synpo−/− preparations (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative electrophysiological measurements.

claim: A significant increase in sEPSC amplitudes was observed in GFP/Synpo expressing pyramidal neurons following atRA treatment.
source: Indeed, a significant increase in sEPSC amplitudes was observed in GFP/Synpo expressing pyramidal neurons following atRA treatment (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological data from rescue experiments.

claim: The presence of synaptopodin is required for atRA-mediated synaptic strengthening.
source: Taken together, we conclude that the presence of synaptopodin is required for atRA-mediated synaptic strengthening.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on data from knockout and rescue experiments.

claim: The biological effects of atRA occur at the levels of gene transcription and mRNA translation.
source: The biological effects of atRA occur at the levels of gene transcription and mRNA translation (i.e., protein synthesis; Drager, 2006; Poon and Chen, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on atRA mechanisms.

claim: A significant increase in the amplitudes of AMPA receptor-mediated sEPSCs was observed in the atRA-treated group in both vehicle-only and actinomycin D co-incubated slices.
source: However, we observed a significant increase in the amplitudes of AMPA receptor-mediated sEPSCs in the atRA-treated group in both vehicle-only and actinomycin D co-incubated slices (Figure 4A,B), thus further confirming that atRA mediates synaptic strengthening.
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological data from pharmacological experiments.

claim: atRA-mediated synaptic strengthening does not require major transcriptional changes.
source: However, we observed a significant increase in the amplitudes of AMPA receptor-mediated sEPSCs in the atRA-treated group in both vehicle-only and actinomycin D co-incubated slices (Figure 4A,B), thus further confirming that atRA mediates synaptic strengthening.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the persistence of atRA effects in the presence of transcription inhibitor.

claim: No significant changes in sEPSC amplitudes were detected in the presence of both atRA and anisomycin.
source: In contrast to our experiments with actinomycin D (Figure 4A), however, no significant changes in sEPSC amplitudes were detected in the presence of both atRA and anisomycin (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological data from pharmacological experiments.

claim: The effects of atRA on excitatory neurotransmission do not require major transcriptional changes, but depend on mRNA translation and protein synthesis.
source: Together, these results indicate that the effects of atRA on excitatory neurotransmission do not require major transcriptional changes, but depend on mRNA translation and protein synthesis.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on pharmacological inhibitor experiments.

claim: No significant differences in sEPSC amplitudes were observed between atRA-treated and vehicle-only groups in human cortical slices when anisomycin was present.
source: No significant differences in sEPSC amplitudes were observed between the two groups (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: The manuscript reports electrophysiological data from human slices with anisomycin.

claim: Anisomycin blocked the atRA-mediated increases in dendritic spine head and synaptopodin cluster sizes.
source: Consistent with these findings, anisomycin also blocked the observed atRA-mediated increases in dendritic spine head and synaptopodin cluster sizes, whereas the sizes of synaptopodin-positive and synaptopodin-negative spine heads remain significantly different (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: The manuscript reports morphological data from human slices with anisomycin.

claim: atRA-mediated plasticity requires mRNA translation to trigger coordinated changes in synaptic strength, spine head size, and synaptopodin cluster properties in cortical slices prepared from the adult human brain.
source: These results demonstrate that atRA-mediated plasticity requires mRNA translation to trigger coordinated changes in synaptic strength, spine head size, and synaptopodin cluster properties in cortical slices prepared from the adult human brain.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on pharmacological inhibitor experiments in human tissue.

claim: Vitamin A and its metabolites bind to nuclear and cytoplasmic receptors and regulate important biological processes, such as cell growth, cell survival, and differentiation.
source: Vitamin A and its metabolites bind to nuclear and cytoplasmic receptors and regulate important biological processes, such as cell growth, cell survival, and differentiation (Al Tanoury et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on vitamin A biology.

claim: atRA is used clinically in dermatology and oncology.
source: Specifically, all-trans retinoic acid (atRA), which is used clinically in dermatology and oncology (Dobrotkova et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2009), has been studied for its neuroprotective and plasticity-promoting effects in animal models (Chen et al., 2014; Koryakina et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on clinical uses of atRA.

claim: atRA has been studied for its neuroprotective and plasticity-promoting effects in animal models.
source: Specifically, all-trans retinoic acid (atRA), which is used clinically in dermatology and oncology (Dobrotkova et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2009), has been studied for its neuroprotective and plasticity-promoting effects in animal models (Chen et al., 2014; Koryakina et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous animal studies on atRA.

claim: Recent studies have evaluated the effects of atRA in patients with brain disorders associated with cognitive dysfunction, including Alzheimer's disease, Fragile X syndrome, and depression.
source: Recent studies have evaluated the effects of atRA in patients with brain disorders associated with cognitive dysfunction, including Alzheimer's disease, Fragile X syndrome, and depression (Bremner et al., 2012; Ding et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent clinical studies on atRA.

claim: Alterations in retinoic acid-mediated synaptic plasticity have been reported in neurons derived from inducible pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) generated from Fragile X syndrome patients.
source: For example, alterations in retinoic acid-mediated synaptic plasticity have been reported in neurons derived from inducible pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) generated from Fragile X syndrome patients (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study on iPSC-derived neurons from patients.

claim: Direct experimental evidence for atRA-mediated effects on synaptic plasticity of principal neurons in the adult human cortex is lacking.
source: However, direct experimental evidence for atRA-mediated effects on synaptic plasticity of principal neurons in the adult human cortex is lacking.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: Direct experimental evidence for coordinated structural and functional synaptic changes in the adult human cortex is lacking.
source: However, direct experimental evidence for coordinated structural and functional synaptic changes in the adult human cortex is lacking (Mansvelder et al., 2019; Verhoog et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work identifying a gap in knowledge.

claim: The ability of neurons to express plasticity by responding to specific stimuli with structural and functional changes is critical for physiological brain function.
source: The ability of neurons to express plasticity by responding to specific stimuli with structural and functional changes is critical for physiological brain function (Citri and Malenka, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about synaptic plasticity.

claim: Cellular and molecular mechanisms of synaptic plasticity have been extensively studied across various animal models over the past few decades.
source: Over the past few decades, cellular and molecular mechanisms of synaptic plasticity have been extensively studied across various animal models (Ho et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work summarizing the field.

claim: The spine apparatus organelle is composed of stacked smooth endoplasmic reticulum and is found in subsets of dendritic spines.
source: This enigmatic cellular organelle is composed of stacked smooth endoplasmic reticulum and is found in subsets of dendritic spines (Kulik et al., 2019; Spacek, 1985).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work characterizing the spine apparatus.

claim: Synaptopodin promotes the accumulation of AMPA receptors at synaptic sites.
source: In this context, we previously showed that synaptopodin promotes the accumulation of AMPA receptors at synaptic sites (Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on synaptopodin function.

claim: atRA and synaptopodin have been linked to AMPA receptor-mediated synaptic plasticity.
source: Given that atRA and synaptopodin have been linked to AMPA receptor-mediated synaptic plasticity (Aoto et al., 2008; Arendt et al., 2015a; Maggio and Vlachos, 2018; Poon and Chen, 2008; Vlachos et al., 2013; Vlachos et al., 2009), we asked whether atRA mediates its effects via synaptopodin and the spine apparatus organelle (Figure 2D–J).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work linking atRA and synaptopodin to AMPA receptors.

claim: Retinoid receptors bound to specific cytoplasmic mRNAs control synaptic plasticity by regulating the synthesis, trafficking, and accumulation of synaptic proteins.
source: Several animal studies have revealed that retinoid receptors bound to specific cytoplasmic mRNAs control synaptic plasticity by regulating the synthesis, trafficking, and accumulation of synaptic proteins (Aoto et al., 2008; Groth and Tsien, 2008; Maghsoodi et al., 2008; Poon and Chen, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous animal studies on retinoid receptor mechanisms.

claim: atRA-mediated structural and functional synaptic plasticity in adult human cortical slices requires mRNA translation.
source: Consistent with recent reports on the importance of protein synthesis in synaptic plasticity (Biever et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2019; Sutton and Schuman, 2006), our experiments revealed that atRA-mediated structural and functional synaptic plasticity in adult human cortical slices requires mRNA translation.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on pharmacological inhibitor experiments.

claim: Synaptopodin is a target and mediator of atRA-induced synaptic plasticity.
source: At the mechanistic level, we identified synaptopodin as a target and mediator of atRA-induced synaptic plasticity.
evidence: The manuscript concludes based on experiments with knockout and rescue mice.

claim: Approximately 70% of dendritic spines in the superficial layers of the human cortex contain synaptopodin clusters.
source: The results of the present study demonstrate that (1) approximately 70% of dendritic spines in the superficial layers of the human cortex contain synaptopodin clusters; (2) synaptopodin is a marker of the human spine apparatus organelle; (3) synaptopodin clusters and spine apparatus organelles are found in large dendritic spines; and (4) a plasticity-inducing stimulus, that is, application of atRA, promotes remodeling of synaptopodin clusters, spine apparatus organelles, and dendritic spines in cortical slices prepared from the adult human brain (c.f., Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes key findings about synaptopodin in human cortex.

claim: Synaptopodin clusters and spine apparatus organelles are found in large dendritic spines.
source: The results of the present study demonstrate that (1) approximately 70% of dendritic spines in the superficial layers of the human cortex contain synaptopodin clusters; (2) synaptopodin is a marker of the human spine apparatus organelle; (3) synaptopodin clusters and spine apparatus organelles are found in large dendritic spines; and (4) a plasticity-inducing stimulus, that is, application of atRA, promotes remodeling of synaptopodin clusters, spine apparatus organelles, and dendritic spines in cortical slices prepared from the adult human brain (c.f., Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes key findings about synaptopodin localization.

claim: Application of atRA promotes remodeling of synaptopodin clusters, spine apparatus organelles, and dendritic spines in cortical slices prepared from the adult human brain.
source: The results of the present study demonstrate that (1) approximately 70% of dendritic spines in the superficial layers of the human cortex contain synaptopodin clusters; (2) synaptopodin is a marker of the human spine apparatus organelle; (3) synaptopodin clusters and spine apparatus organelles are found in large dendritic spines; and (4) a plasticity-inducing stimulus, that is, application of atRA, promotes remodeling of synaptopodin clusters, spine apparatus organelles, and dendritic spines in cortical slices prepared from the adult human brain (c.f., Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes key findings about atRA effects.

claim: A role of the spine apparatus organelle in local protein synthesis and the regulation of intracellular calcium dynamics has been suggested.
source: The involvement of synaptopodin and the spine apparatus organelle in synaptic plasticity is still enigmatic; however, a role in local protein synthesis and the regulation of intracellular calcium dynamics have been suggested (Fifková et al., 1983; Pierce et al., 2000).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on spine apparatus function.

claim: Synaptopodin binds to actin and α-actinin and has been suggested to orchestrate spine dynamics via Rho-A signaling and long-term spine stability.
source: Synaptopodin binds to actin and α-actinin and has been suggested to orchestrate spine dynamics via Rho-A signaling and long-term spine stability (Asanuma et al., 2006; Yap et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on synaptopodin molecular interactions.

claim: Synaptopodin and myosin V are associated.
source: More recently, synaptopodin and myosin V were reported to be associated (Konietzny et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent work on synaptopodin interactions.

claim: Synaptopodin may link spine actin and myosin to spine apparatus organelles.
source: However, the strategic positioning of synaptopodin clusters in the head, neck, and base of murine and human dendritic spines indicates that this molecule may act primarily within or in association with the spine compartment. Here, synaptopodin may link spine actin and myosin to spine apparatus organelles, which have a more restricted localization (Konietzny et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript speculates based on localization data and previous work.

claim: The rapid/initial atRA-mediated spine enlargement does not require the actual presence of synaptopodin clusters (spine apparatus organelles).
source: In support of this hypothesis, atRA application in our study triggered changes in spine head size in both synaptopodin-positive and synaptopodin-negative spines from human cortical slices, suggesting that the rapid/initial atRA-mediated spine enlargement does not require the actual presence of synaptopodin clusters, that is, spine apparatus organelles (Okubo-Suzuki et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript infers this from the observation that both spine types respond to atRA.

claim: Synaptopodin clusters are highly dynamic structures that can change their position within spines, and may appear in existing spines.
source: Considering that synaptopodin clusters are highly dynamic structures that can change their position within spines, and may appear in existing spines (Vlachos et al., 2009; Yap et al., 2020), it is interesting to speculate that atRA may trigger a molecular cascade that promotes rapid spine growth, even in spines that do not contain a spine apparatus organelle, eventually leading to the formation and enlargement of spine apparatus organelles.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on synaptopodin dynamics.

claim: atRA may trigger a molecular cascade that promotes rapid spine growth, even in spines that do not contain a spine apparatus organelle, eventually leading to the formation and enlargement of spine apparatus organelles.
source: Considering that synaptopodin clusters are highly dynamic structures that can change their position within spines, and may appear in existing spines (Vlachos et al., 2009; Yap et al., 2020), it is interesting to speculate that atRA may trigger a molecular cascade that promotes rapid spine growth, even in spines that do not contain a spine apparatus organelle, eventually leading to the formation and enlargement of spine apparatus organelles.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about the temporal sequence of atRA effects.

claim: Both atRA and synaptopodin have been linked to the expression of Hebbian and homeostatic synaptic plasticity in rodent brain tissue.
source: Both atRA and synaptopodin have been linked to the expression of Hebbian and homeostatic synaptic plasticity in rodent brain tissue and are associated with Ca2+-dependent AMPA receptor synthesis and trafficking (Arendt et al., 2015b; Vlachos et al., 2013; Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on atRA and synaptopodin in plasticity.

claim: atRA and synaptopodin are associated with Ca2+-dependent AMPA receptor synthesis and trafficking.
source: Both atRA and synaptopodin have been linked to the expression of Hebbian and homeostatic synaptic plasticity in rodent brain tissue and are associated with Ca2+-dependent AMPA receptor synthesis and trafficking (Arendt et al., 2015b; Vlachos et al., 2013; Vlachos et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on molecular mechanisms.

claim: Alterations in retinoid signaling and synaptopodin expression have been associated with synaptic plasticity defects in pathological brain states.
source: In turn, alterations in retinoid signaling and synaptopodin expression have been associated with synaptic plasticity defects in pathological brain states (Bremner et al., 2012; Maggio and Vlachos, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous work on pathological conditions.

claim: Increased sEPSC amplitudes and frequencies were observed in the cortical neurons of synaptopodin-deficient mice.
source: Considering that increased sEPSC amplitudes and frequencies were observed in the cortical neurons of Synpo−/− mice, it would be interesting to evaluate whether alterations in retinoid metabolism are present in this mouse model.
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from knockout mice.

claim: Alterations in synaptopodin expression and retinoid signaling have been observed in the brain tissue of patients with Alzheimer's disease and cognitive decline.
source: Accordingly, alterations in synaptopodin expression and retinoid signaling have been observed in the brain tissue of patients with Alzheimer's disease and cognitive decline (Goodman, 2006; Goodman and Pardee, 2003; Mingaud et al., 2008; Misner et al., 2001; Reddy et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous clinical studies.

claim: Retinoids have been proposed as a potential therapeutic avenue for Alzheimer's disease-associated cognitive decline.
source: Given that retinoids have been proposed as a potential therapeutic avenue for Alzheimer's disease-associated cognitive decline (Ding et al., 2008; Endres et al., 2014), it is conceivable that atRA may act – at least in part – by modulating synaptopodin expression, thereby improving the ability of adult human cortical neurons to express synaptic plasticity.

claim: atRA may act by modulating synaptopodin expression, thereby improving the ability of adult human cortical neurons to express synaptic plasticity.
